lesson.title: Asking and Answering: How HTTP Moves the Web
lesson.summary: HTTP is the application layer protocol that lets a client ask a server for something and get a response back, built on top of TCP and precisely defined by RFC documents so independently written software can interoperate.
lesson.body:
Everything discussed so far in this chapter set, DNS in all its forms, exists to answer one question: what address should a client connect to. HTTP is what happens after that address is found. It is an application layer protocol, meaning it defines the format of the actual conversation between a web client and a web server, not how bytes get physically moved between them. The model is simple to state: a client sends a request naming something it wants, and a server sends back a response, either the thing itself or an explanation of why it cannot provide it.

HTTP does not handle its own delivery. It is built on top of TCP, and it depends completely on what TCP provides: a reliable, ordered, connection oriented stream of bytes between the two ends. Before a single HTTP request byte is sent, TCP has already completed its three way handshake and established that connection. Because TCP guarantees the bytes arrive in order and retransmits anything lost, HTTP itself does not have to worry about any of that. It can stay a relatively simple, mostly text based protocol, focused entirely on what to ask for and how to describe the answer, while TCP quietly handles getting the bytes there intact.

A second foundational property of HTTP is that it is stateless. Each request is handled on its own, and by default a server has no memory that a given request came from the same client as some earlier request. That sounds like a limitation, and it is, but it is a deliberate one that keeps the core protocol simple, and later chapters on headers and cookies cover exactly how real applications build persistent sessions on top of a protocol that itself remembers nothing.

None of this behavior is informal convention. HTTP is precisely specified in RFC documents published through the IETF, starting with HTTP/1.0 in RFC 1945 and then HTTP/1.1 in RFC 2616, later refined into a more modular set of RFCs. Because the rules are written down in that much detail, a browser built by one organization and a web server built by a completely different one can exchange requests and responses correctly without either ever having to guess at the other's behavior.

A minimal exchange makes the model concrete. Over an already open TCP connection to port 80, a client might send:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com

and the server might reply:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 137

followed by the actual HTML for the page. That single request and response, one asking and one answering, is the whole pattern. The next several chapters unpack each piece of it: the verbs a request can use, the status codes a response can return, the headers that carry metadata like the ones already shown here, and the version details specific to HTTP/1.1 itself.
